title: Following One Block
move: decide which lines run repeatedly, which run once afterward, and what each name points at on every pass.

adds.text: Until now every line ran exactly once, in written order. A `for` line breaks that, and it breaks it in a way that is entirely visible on the page: the colon and the indentation tell you which lines repeat. Nothing about the object model changes. Names are bound and objects are changed exactly as before — just more than once.

blocks.text:
for item in [10, 20, 30]:
    print(item)
Read it aloud as: *"For each value that comes out of this collection, point the name `item` at it, then run the indented lines."*
Three things are worth noticing immediately:

items: `item` is an ordinary name. The `for` line **rebinds** it before each pass — the same event as any assignment.
The colon at the end says *a block starts here*.
The indented lines are the **body**. They run once per pass.

ideas.title: Indentation is the block, and nothing else is

blocks.text: `print("inside", n)` is indented, so it belongs to the loop and runs three times. `print("after")` is back at the left margin, so the loop is over by the time it runs, and it runs once. Move that last line four spaces right and the program prints "after" three times. Indentation is not decoration; it *is* the structure.
Python is strict about it: a block's lines must be indented consistently, and mixing tabs and spaces is an error rather than a style complaint.
The way to make a loop concrete before you have any vocabulary for it is to number the lines in the order Python actually reaches them:

total = 0                    # 1
for n in [5, 7]:             # 2, 4, 6
    total = total + n        # 3, 5
print(total)                 # 7

Reading that: line 2 runs to fetch 5; line 3 runs; line 2 runs again to fetch 7; line 3 runs again; line 2 runs a *third* time, finds nothing left, and the loop ends; line 4 runs once. The `for` line runs one more time than the body does — that final pass is the one that discovers there is nothing left.
For anything longer than two lines, write a table with one row per pass:
The last row matters: **the loop name still exists after the loop**, still pointing at the final value. `for` does not clean up after itself.

`range(n)` produces the numbers from 0 up to but not including `n`. `range(a, b)` goes from `a` up to but not including `b`. `range(a, b, step)` counts by `step`. `range(3)` gives 0, 1, 2 — three numbers, starting at zero.

A `range` is not a list. `print(range(3))` shows `range(0, 3)`, not `[0, 1, 2]`, because a range does not build its numbers in advance — it produces each one as the loop asks for it. This is why `range(10000000)` costs nothing to create. Use `list(range(3))` when you genuinely want the list.

total = 0
for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    total = total + n
print(total)          # 6

The name `total` must be bound **before** the loop, because the first pass reads it. Each pass rebinds it. The post-loop line reads the last binding. Almost every loop you write is a variation on this shape, with `total = 0` replaced by `results = []` and the body doing `results.append(...)`.

ideas.title: Rebinding the loop name does not touch the collection

blocks.text:
xs = [1, 2, 3]
for x in xs:
    x = x * 2
print(xs)             # [1, 2, 3]
Each pass points `x` at an item, then points `x` somewhere else. The list's slots were never involved — nothing wrote into `xs`. Compare:

grid = [[1], [2]]
for row in grid:
    row.append(0)
print(grid)           # [[1, 0], [2, 0]]
Here the body *changes* the object `row` points at, and that object is the same one sitting in the list's slot. Stage 2's distinction, now with a loop wrapped around it.
To actually replace items, write the slots by position:

xs = [1, 2, 3]
for i in range(len(xs)):
    xs[i] = xs[i] * 2
print(xs)             # [2, 4, 6]

items: `break` stops the loop immediately. The loop's remaining passes never happen, and Python continues at the first unindented line after the loop.
`continue` abandons the *rest of the body* for this pass only and goes back to the `for` line for the next value.

blocks.text: Both affect **the one loop they are directly inside**. That qualifier does nothing yet, because there is only one loop; it becomes the whole point in Stage 7.

ideas.title: Changing a list while looping over it

blocks.text: The loop walks by position while the list is shrinking underneath it, so positions shift and some items are never examined. The result is not random — it is perfectly predictable if you trace it — but it is almost never what the author meant. The habit: **build a new list instead of editing the one you are looping over.**

blocks.text: **With `xs = [[0]] * 2`:** `[[2]]` repeated — the printed result is `[[2], [2]]`.

With two distinct inner lists, each pass writes slot 0 of a different list, and each goes from 0 to 1. With one shared inner list, the body runs twice on *the same object*: first pass makes it `[1]`, second pass reads that `1` and makes it `[2]`. Both slots then show `[2]`.
This is the Stage 4 pitfall with a loop over it, and it is the version that actually appears in real code — the doubling is what makes it obvious that the body ran twice on one object.
That sharing merely duplicates a display, rather than compounding repeated changes.

answer.text: `x = 0` rebinds the loop name to the number 0 and never touches the list's slots, so the list is unchanged; the smallest working alternative is `for i in range(len(xs)): xs[i] = 0`. **Error type if missed:** object-model. Go back to 5.7 and 5.9.
